analysis.title: Mind on the Market: The Race to Build AI Infrastructure Continues
key_insights: Hyperscaler capital expenditures (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle, Meta) have grown faster than their free cash flow as they invest in chips and data centers. Hyperscaler YoY capex growth is +86.5% as of 6/30/2026.
The late-1990s telecom boom is used as an analogy: investment expands capacity, and expanding capacity can move scarcity and economic rents to other parts of the ecosystem.
Fiber builders Global Crossing and WorldCom financed the buildout aggressively and later entered bankruptcy, while much of the long-term value went to firms that used the abundant connectivity.

Within the US AI stack, compute and data-center capacity have scaled rapidly. Power and cooling, grid and transmission, and enterprise-wide adoption are at earlier stages, so progress in one layer can expose a constraint in another.
No country controls the whole AI stack. The US leads in AI models and hyperscale computing, Taiwan in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, and South Korea in memory technologies.
The Netherlands, Canada and Germany also offer exposure to key AI-related industries, so AI leadership may broaden across countries as well as industries.

Companies that attract capital invite competition, which gradually reduces scarcity. Falling unit costs may speed adoption but make it harder for undifferentiated infrastructure providers to sustain margins.
Investors are advised to separate volume growth from economic rent capture. Strong demand does not necessarily produce attractive returns on incremental capital.
Value may move toward companies that use AI rather than those that build it, with healthcare, financials and industrials named as possible long-term beneficiaries.

Consensus EPS growth for Information Technology is 41.8% for 2026-2027 versus 26.8% for 2027-2028. Health Care has the second-strongest near-term growth and a sharper slowdown by 2028, while Industrials and Financials stay comparatively resilient and improve into 2028.

Investment implication: near-term AI infrastructure demand is strong, but the scale of spending raises the hurdle for returns. Investors should check whether capacity stays differentiated and whether AI revenues earn attractive returns on incremental capital.

tension_points.bull_case: Near-term demand for AI infrastructure remains powerful, and compute and cloud capacity carry real scarcity. Hyperscaler capex is up +86.5% YoY.
tension_points.bear_case: Capex is outgrowing free cash flow, and capital invites competition that erodes scarcity. As in the telecom boom, strong demand does not necessarily mean attractive returns on incremental capital.

theme_stances.key_argument: Today's AI infrastructure builders may not be tomorrow's primary beneficiaries, as economic rents migrate to companies that use the technology.
theme_stances.evidence: today's builders may not be tomorrow's primary beneficiaries
